title: The Lasombra of Iberia
summary: Magister rule split by the Reconquista.

claims.text: Iberia is the heartland of Clan Lasombra, and the Magisters long stood united to show that every other Cainite feeds there at their pleasure.
The war between Christians and Muslims divides them: devout Muslim Lasombra fight to save al-Andalus while their Christian kin pursue the Shadow Reconquista.
That unity held until the end of the eleventh century; its first crack came when the Amici Noctis would not allow the Embrace of the Muslim leader al-Mansur on their terms.
Brujah, Lasombra and Ventrue used the Visigothic invasion to fight one another: the Ventrue sought a return of Roman order and the Brujah a new Iberian identity.
The Lasombra held back and let their rivals wear each other down while keeping hold of mortal institutions, which began an age of Magister supremacy.
In A.D. 585 Ventrue raiders destroyed the Brujah elder Yzebel in what becomes northern Portugal, sealing the fate of both Brujah and Ventrue in Iberia.

title: Cainites among the taifas
summary: Power shifts after the fall of Cordoba’s authority.

claims.text: When Cordoban rule collapsed, the Assamite Hilel al-Masaari could no longer enforce a claim to the whole domain, and other sultans rose.
In Granada the Lasombra Badr came to notice, while in Cordoba the Lasombra intriguer Miriam bint Aisha publicly backed al-Masaari and privately spun a web of influence.
The Assamite vizier Umar al-Rashid helped prepare the Almoravid invasion, settled in Sevilla and backed the Brujah Gerusah bint Yoav as sultan; Umar and Miriam remain rivals.
Iberian Lasombra came close to worshipping El Cid as an image of their ideals of decisive action.

title: After Las Navas de Tolosa
summary: The Muslim taifas left after the great battle.

claims.text: After Las Navas de Tolosa the Christian frontier pushes rapidly south, and a power vacuum opens in Muslim lands.
Murcia becomes a centre of resistance and a refuge for Ashirra bands, while Arjona becomes a vassal of Castile and even helps it against other Muslim states.
Ashirra, Arabic for brethren, is the name Islamic Cainites use; the loose sect holds that Islam offers vampires a hope of salvation.
Its guidelines include nightly prayers, almsgiving and a kind of blood fast in Ramadan.
Since the Qur’an forbids drinking blood, most purify it in a bowl while praying for forgiveness and feed from healthy herds; others say jihad outweighs the sin.

title: The Lions of Rodrigo
summary: Brutal knights of the Shadow Reconquista.

claims.text: From the Pyrenees to the Atlas the Lions of Rodrigo are known as some of the most violent knights fighting for the Shadow Reconquista.
Some Cainites think their thirst for blood outruns their piety, and diablerized Cainites have turned up in havens near their campaigns.
By their own account the knights feed solely on heretics and enemies of the Church.

title: The Apostles of the Third Caine
summary: A reform sect of the Cainite Heresy.

claims.text: The Apostles broke from the See of Nod around the year 1000, believing Narses of Venice, then Archbishop of Nod, cared too much for worldly matters.
Like the reforming monastic orders, they live austerely and hope to draw other Heretics away to prepare for the coming vampiric Messiah.
The Sword of St. James is a band of Christian men devoted to rooting out supernatural evil, distinct from the Knights of Santiago.
The Iberian noble Rodrigue de Navarre founded it after stumbling on the Cainite Heresy, and has gathered evidence since 1190 that creatures of the night use mortals as pawns.
